title: Sim-to-Real Transfer
definition: Training policies $\pi_\theta(a|s)$ in simulation and deploying them on real robots. The reality gap — differences in physics, rendering, dynamics, and sensor noise between sim and real — causes policies to fail when transferred. Formally, we train in an MDP $\mathcal{M}_{\text{sim}} = (\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, T_{\text{sim}}, R, \gamma)$ but deploy in $\mathcal{M}_{\text{real}} = (\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, T_{\text{real}}, R, \gamma)$ where $T_{\text{sim}} \neq T_{\text{real}}$. Bridged via domain randomization, system identification, or fine-tuning.
intuition: Like training a pilot only on a flight simulator, then putting them in a real cockpit. The simulator doesn't perfectly model turbulence, weather, or instrument lag. Domain randomization is like training in hundreds of slightly wrong simulators — the pilot learns to handle anything because no single sim was 'right.'
practical_example: Training a robot hand to rotate a Rubik's cube (OpenAI, 2019). Policy trained in Isaac Gym with massive domain randomization: friction $\mu \in [0.5\mu_0, 1.5\mu_0]$, mass $m \in [0.7m_0, 1.3m_0]$, joint damping $d \in [0.6d_0, 1.4d_0]$, visual texture randomization. $10^{11}$ sim steps, transferred zero-shot to real robot with ~70% success.
failure_mode: Reality gap too large: sim dynamics $T_{\text{sim}}(s'|s,a)$ don't capture real contact modes (e.g., soft deformable objects, liquids, articulated mechanisms). Symptoms: policy works perfectly in sim but fails immediately on real robot. Fix: improve sim fidelity for critical dynamics, use residual RL ($\pi_{\text{real}}(a|s) = \pi_{\text{sim}}(a|s) + \Delta\pi_{\text{residual}}(a|s)$), or switch to real-world fine-tuning.
interview_answer: Sim2real is the dominant paradigm for robot learning because real-world data is expensive and risky. The core challenge is the reality gap: $T_{\text{sim}} \neq T_{\text{real}}$. Domain randomization is the most practical solution: randomize physics params, visual appearance, and dynamics during training so the policy becomes robust to sim-real mismatch. Key implementation: randomize the parameters that matter most for your task (contact dynamics for manipulation, terrain for locomotion). Complementary approaches: system identification to narrow the randomization range, and residual policies $\pi = \pi_{\text{sim}} + \Delta\pi$ for real-world fine-tuning.

title: Domain Randomization
definition: Training with randomized simulation parameters $\xi \sim \mathcal{U}(\Xi)$ so the policy treats the real world as just another random variation. The objective becomes: $$\pi^* = \arg\max_\pi \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim p(\xi)} \left[ \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi, T_\xi} \left[ \sum_{t=0}^H \gamma^t R(s_t, a_t) \right] \right]$$ Parameters randomized include: mass $m$, friction $\mu$, damping $d$, visual textures, lighting, camera pose, observation noise $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, action delays $\Delta t$.
intuition: If you learn to cook in 1000 different kitchens — different stoves, different pans, different temperatures — you'll handle any new kitchen because you've seen enough variation. The real world is just kitchen #1001. The key: randomize enough that reality falls within your training distribution.
practical_example: Sim2real for robotic grasping: randomize object mass $m \in [0.01, 2.0]$ kg, friction $\mu \in [0.3, 1.0]$, table height $h \pm 5$ cm, camera position $\pm 2$ cm, lighting direction, gripper finger friction. Train with PPO across 1024 parallel environments. The policy learns invariance to all these factors.
failure_mode: Randomization range too wide: policy becomes overly conservative, performing worst-case behavior everywhere. Randomization range too narrow: doesn't cover real-world variation, i.e., $\xi_{\text{real}} \notin \Xi$. Symptoms: either cautious/slow policy or failed transfer. Fix: use automatic domain randomization (ADR) that expands ranges based on performance thresholds $\phi$, or use system identification to set realistic ranges.
interview_answer: Domain randomization makes sim2real work at scale. The insight: if the policy has seen enough variation during training, the real world becomes just another sample from the training distribution $p(\xi)$. In practice, I randomize physics ($m, \mu, d$), dynamics (action delay $\Delta t$, control frequency), and visual properties (textures, lighting, camera). The critical design choice is the randomization distribution — too narrow and $\xi_{\text{real}} \notin \Xi$, too wide and the policy becomes conservative. ADR (Automatic Domain Randomization) addresses this by expanding ranges when the policy exceeds a success threshold and narrowing when it fails.

title: Behavior Cloning (BC)
definition: Supervised learning on expert demonstrations: learn $\pi_\theta(a|s)$ directly from $(s_i, a_i)$ pairs collected by an expert $\pi^*$. The objective is: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{BC}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(s,a) \sim \mathcal{D}_{\text{expert}}} \left[ \| \pi_\theta(s) - a \|^2 \right]$$ Simple and effective when demonstrations are plentiful and the state space is well-covered. Suffers from compounding errors due to covariate shift: training on $d_{\pi^*}(s)$ but executing under $d_{\pi_\theta}(s)$.
intuition: Like learning to drive by watching dashcam footage of a good driver and imitating their steering at each frame. Works great for situations the expert demonstrated. But the moment you drift slightly off the expert's trajectory — perhaps due to a minor prediction error — you enter states the expert never showed you, and errors compound: small drift → unfamiliar state → bigger error → more unfamiliar state.
practical_example: Learning a 6-DOF pick-and-place policy from 100 teleoperated demonstrations. With image observations and a ResNet encoder: BC achieves 60% success. Adding data augmentation (random crops, color jitter) brings it to 75%. DAgger with 20 additional corrective demonstrations reaches 90%. The compounding error grows as $\mathcal{O}(T^2)$ in the horizon length $T$ for standard BC.
failure_mode: Covariate shift / compounding errors: the policy makes a small error $\epsilon$ at each step, entering states where $d_{\pi_\theta}(s) \neq d_{\pi^*}(s)$, causing the total error to grow as $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon T^2)$ over horizon $T$. Symptoms: works in easy cases but fails on slight perturbations, degrades over longer horizons. Fix: use DAgger (online expert correction), add noise during data collection, use action chunking, or switch to offline RL.
interview_answer: BC is the simplest imitation learning approach — supervised learning minimizing $\|\pi_\theta(s) - a^*\|^2$ on expert $(s, a)$ pairs. It works surprisingly well when you have enough diverse demonstrations and the right architecture. The fundamental limitation is compounding errors from covariate shift: the learned state distribution $d_{\pi_\theta}$ diverges from the expert distribution $d_{\pi^*}$, with error growing as $\mathcal{O}(T^2)$. Practical fixes: DAgger for online correction, action chunking (predicting sequences of $K$ actions rather than single actions), data augmentation, and collecting demonstrations with intentional perturbations. For industry, BC is often the first thing to try — if it works with 50-100 demos, you've saved months over RL.

title: Action Chunking for Manipulation
definition: Instead of predicting a single action $a_t$ per timestep, predict a sequence (chunk) of $K$ future actions $\{a_t, a_{t+1}, \ldots, a_{t+K-1}\}$ at once. The policy becomes $\pi_\theta: s_t \mapsto (a_t, a_{t+1}, \ldots, a_{t+K-1})$. Reduces the effective decision horizon from $T$ to $T/K$, mitigates compounding errors in BC (error scales as $\mathcal{O}((T/K)^2)$ instead of $\mathcal{O}(T^2)$), and produces smoother trajectories. Used in ACT (Action Chunking with Transformers) and diffusion policies.
intuition: Instead of giving turn-by-turn GPS directions one step at a time, you give the next 10 steps at once. The driver can plan smoother turns because they see the upcoming trajectory. If one step is slightly off, the remaining chunk keeps them on track rather than going off-course.
practical_example: ACT (Action Chunking with Transformers) for bimanual manipulation: predict chunks of $K=100$ timesteps (2 seconds at 50Hz). A CVAE encoder models the latent style variable $z \sim q_\phi(z|\tau)$ to capture multi-modal behavior, transformer decoder generates the chunk $\{a_t\}_{t=0}^{K-1}$ conditioned on $(s, z)$. Temporal ensembling blends overlapping chunks with exponential weights $w_i = \exp(-\alpha \cdot i)$. Achieves near-human performance on complex bimanual tasks with only 50 demonstrations.
failure_mode: Chunk too long ($K$ too large): can't react to unexpected perturbations or dynamic changes because actions are committed in advance. Chunk too short ($K$ too small): loses the compounding error benefit. Also: temporal blending between consecutive chunks can cause jittery behavior if not done carefully. Fix: use exponential weighting $w_i = \exp(-\alpha \cdot i)$ for chunk blending, choose $K$ based on task reactivity needs.
interview_answer: Action chunking addresses the compounding error problem in behavior cloning by predicting sequences of $K$ actions rather than one at a time. The key insight: predicting $K$ steps at once reduces the effective decision horizon from $T$ to $T/K$, so compounding error scales as $\mathcal{O}((T/K)^2)$ instead of $\mathcal{O}(T^2)$. In ACT, $K=100$ works well for manipulation tasks. Combined with temporal ensembling (blending overlapping chunks via exponential weights), it produces smooth, robust trajectories. This idea is also central to diffusion policies, which generate entire action chunks via iterative denoising from $a^{(N)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ to $a^{(0)}$.

title: Visuomotor Policies
definition: End-to-end policies $\pi_\theta: \mathcal{O}_{\text{image}} \rightarrow \mathcal{A}$ that map raw visual observations (RGB/RGB-D images) directly to motor commands without hand-designed perception pipelines. Typically: CNN/ViT encoder $f_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$ → spatial features → policy head (MLP or transformer) $g_\psi: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathcal{A}$ → actions.
intuition: Instead of building separate perception (detect object) → planning (compute grasp) → control (execute motion) modules, you train one neural network that sees the camera image and outputs joint velocities. Like teaching someone to catch a ball by practice rather than by explaining physics equations.
practical_example: ResNet-18 encoder with spatial softmax $\text{softmax}(f_{ij}) \rightarrow (x_c, y_c)$ → 64-dim feature → MLP → 7-DOF joint velocities $\dot{q} \in \mathbb{R}^7$ for pick-and-place. Trained on 200 teleoperated demonstrations with random crops for augmentation. Key: spatial softmax preserves spatial structure (outputting expected 2D coordinates) better than global average pooling for manipulation tasks.
failure_mode: Visual overfitting: policy memorizes specific visual features (table texture, lighting) rather than task-relevant structure. The encoder $f_\phi$ fits spurious correlations in the training visuals. Symptoms: works in training environment, fails with any visual change. Fix: aggressive data augmentation (random crops, color jitter, background randomization), use pre-trained frozen vision encoders (R3M, CLIP, DINOv2) so $f_\phi$ is already robust.
interview_answer: Visuomotor policies $\pi_\theta(a | o_{\text{img}})$ are the standard approach for learning manipulation from images. The key architectural choices: use a pre-trained vision encoder $f_\phi$ (DINOv2 or R3M) rather than training from scratch, add spatial features via spatial softmax (not just global pooling), and apply heavy data augmentation. For sample efficiency, pre-trained encoders are a game-changer — they reduce the demo requirement from thousands to tens. The main risk is visual overfitting, which is addressed by augmentation and domain randomization. In practice, I prefer frozen pre-trained encoders with a lightweight policy head $g_\psi$ for most manipulation tasks.

title: DAgger (Dataset Aggregation)
definition: An iterative imitation learning algorithm that addresses covariate shift in behavior cloning by aggregating expert-corrected data from the learner's own state distribution. At iteration $i$: (1) execute current policy $\pi_i$ to collect states $\{s_t\}$, (2) query the expert $\pi^*$ for actions at those states, (3) aggregate $\mathcal{D}_{i+1} = \mathcal{D}_i \cup \{(s_t, \pi^*(s_t))\}$, (4) retrain $\pi_{i+1} = \arg\min_\pi \mathcal{L}(\pi, \mathcal{D}_{i+1})$. Provably reduces the error bound from $\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$ (BC) to $\mathcal{O}(T \epsilon)$ where $\epsilon$ is the single-step error and $T$ is the horizon.
intuition: A student driver first watches an instructor, then drives themselves while the instructor sits in the passenger seat calling out what they would do at each moment. After each drive, the student studies both the original demonstrations and the instructor's corrections from the student's own mistakes. Over rounds, the student sees corrections for exactly the situations they tend to get into.
practical_example: Robot learning a peg insertion task: BC on 50 demos gives 45% success. DAgger round 1: run the BC policy, expert labels corrections at 30 failure states → retrain on 80 total examples → 65% success. Round 2: 20 more corrections → 85% success. Round 3: 10 corrections → 93% success. Key practical detail: use a mixing policy $\pi_i = \beta_i \pi^* + (1-\beta_i) \hat{\pi}_i$ with $\beta_i \rightarrow 0$ to ensure initial data collection is safe.
failure_mode: Expert availability: DAgger requires an on-call expert to label $\pi^*(a|s)$ at arbitrary states, which is expensive for real-robot tasks (human teleoperator must provide corrections in real-time). Expert inconsistency: human experts give noisy, inconsistent labels, especially for states far from the demonstration distribution. Symptoms: improvement plateaus or the policy oscillates between rounds. Fix: use HG-DAgger (human-gated) where the expert only intervenes when needed, or EnsembleDAgger which uses model uncertainty $\text{Var}_{\theta}[\pi_\theta(s)]$ to decide when to query.
interview_answer: DAgger solves the fundamental covariate shift problem in BC by iteratively collecting expert corrections under the learner's own state distribution. The key theoretical result: it reduces the imitation gap from $\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$ to $\mathcal{O}(T \epsilon)$. In practice, the bottleneck is expert availability — you need a human to provide corrections in real-time. Practical variants: HG-DAgger (human intervenes only when policy is about to fail), EnsembleDAgger (query based on epistemic uncertainty), and SafeDAgger (use a safety policy to prevent catastrophic states). For robotics, I typically run 3-5 DAgger rounds with 10-30 corrections each, which often doubles success rate over pure BC.

title: Imitation Learning (Overview)
definition: Learning a policy $\pi_\theta(a|s)$ from expert demonstrations $\mathcal{D} = \{\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_N\}$ where $\tau_i = \{(s_0, a_0), \ldots, (s_T, a_T)\}$. Two main paradigms: (1) Behavioral cloning — supervised learning minimizing $\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{(s,a) \sim \mathcal{D}}[\ell(\pi_\theta(s), a)]$, and (2) Inverse RL (IRL) — recover a reward function $r_\psi(s,a)$ such that $\pi^*$ is optimal, then optimize $\pi_\theta$ under $r_\psi$. IRL solves: $$\max_\psi \left( \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi^*}\left[\sum_t r_\psi(s_t, a_t)\right] - \max_\pi \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi}\left[\sum_t r_\psi(s_t, a_t)\right] \right)$$ Modern methods also include GAIL, which matches state-action distributions via adversarial training.
intuition: Two ways to learn from watching a chef: (1) mimic their exact hand movements at each step (behavior cloning), or (2) figure out what they're optimizing for — flavor, presentation, efficiency — and then optimize for that yourself (inverse RL). The first is simpler but brittle; the second transfers better because you understand the 'why' behind the actions.
practical_example: Comparison on a contact-rich peg-in-hole task with 100 human demonstrations: BC achieves 60% success, DAgger reaches 90% with 3 rounds of corrections, GAIL reaches 80% but needs $10^6$ environment steps for the RL inner loop, IRL (MaxEntIRL) recovers a reward that enables 85% success and generalizes to new peg shapes unseen in demos. In practice, BC + action chunking often matches or beats IRL/GAIL with far less compute, which is why diffusion-policy-style BC has become dominant.
failure_mode: BC: covariate shift with $\mathcal{O}(T^2)$ compounding errors. IRL: reward ambiguity — many reward functions $r_\psi$ explain the same demonstrations, making the problem ill-posed without strong priors. GAIL: requires online environment interaction and is sample-inefficient ($10^5$-$10^7$ steps). Multi-modal demonstrations: when experts use different strategies for the same state, unimodal BC (MSE loss) averages modes, producing an action that corresponds to no valid strategy. Fix: use mixture density networks, diffusion policies, or CVAE-based architectures to capture multi-modality.
interview_answer: Imitation learning is the family of methods for learning from demonstrations. BC is the simplest — minimize $\|\pi_\theta(s) - a^*\|^2$ — but suffers $\mathcal{O}(T^2)$ compounding errors. DAgger fixes this by iteratively collecting expert corrections, reducing error to $\mathcal{O}(T)$. IRL recovers a transferable reward function but is computationally expensive and ill-posed. GAIL matches occupancy measures via adversarial training: $\min_\pi \max_D \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\log D(s,a)] + \mathbb{E}_{\pi^*}[\log(1-D(s,a))]$. In modern robotics, the dominant approach is BC with expressive policy architectures (diffusion policies, transformers with action chunking) that handle multi-modality and long horizons, often outperforming IRL/GAIL with orders of magnitude less compute.

title: Contact-Rich Manipulation
definition: Manipulation tasks involving sustained, complex contact interactions between the robot and objects — e.g., peg insertion, gear meshing, surface wiping, pivoting, in-hand reorientation. Contact dynamics are governed by complementarity constraints: $$0 \leq \lambda_n \perp \phi(q) \geq 0$$ where $\lambda_n$ is the normal contact force and $\phi(q)$ is the signed distance function. Friction follows Coulomb's law $\|f_t\| \leq \mu \lambda_n$ with the maximum dissipation principle. These interactions are discontinuous, making contact-rich tasks fundamentally harder to simulate, plan for, and learn.
intuition: Imagine threading a needle: you can't just plan a trajectory in free space — you must feel the needle against the fabric, adjust force and angle based on tactile feedback, and maintain precise force control while moving. Every millimeter of insertion involves complex friction and deformation. This is qualitatively different from pick-and-place where contacts are brief and simple.
practical_example: Industrial peg-in-hole insertion with $< 0.5$ mm clearance. Approach: learn a residual policy $\pi_{\text{res}}(a|s, f)$ that takes force-torque readings $f \in \mathbb{R}^6$ alongside visual state and outputs corrections $\Delta x \in SE(3)$ on top of a nominal impedance controller $a = K_p(x_{\text{des}} - x) + K_d(\dot{x}_{\text{des}} - \dot{x}) + \pi_{\text{res}}(s, f)$. Trained with 200 demonstrations + DAgger corrections. Key: impedance control provides passive compliance ($F = K(x_0 - x)$ with tunable stiffness $K$), while the learned policy handles the strategy.
failure_mode: Sim2real gap is worst for contact-rich tasks because simulators poorly model: (1) contact patch geometry (point contact vs. distributed), (2) stick-slip friction transitions, (3) deformable object dynamics, (4) force-torque sensor noise and bias. The gap in contact forces can be orders of magnitude: $\|F_{\text{sim}} - F_{\text{real}}\| \gg 0$. Symptoms: policy jams, applies excessive force, or oscillates at contact. Fix: use compliant control as the base layer (impedance/admittance control with gains $K_p, K_d$), add tactile sensing, collect real-world corrections via DAgger, and use low-frequency control ($\leq 20$ Hz) so contact transients are filtered.
interview_answer: Contact-rich manipulation is the frontier challenge in robot learning because contact dynamics are discontinuous ($\phi(q) = 0$ boundary), hard to simulate, and require tight coupling of perception and force control. My approach: (1) Use impedance control $F = K_p e + K_d \dot{e}$ as the compliant base layer for safety and passivity, (2) Learn a residual policy on top that handles task strategy, conditioned on force-torque observations $f \in \mathbb{R}^6$, (3) Train in sim with domain randomization on contact parameters ($\mu, K_{\text{contact}}, \text{damping}$), then refine with real-world DAgger. Tactile sensing (e.g., GelSight providing contact geometry at $\sim$30 Hz) is a game-changer for tasks where vision is occluded during contact. The key insight: don't try to learn contact dynamics end-to-end — let classical compliance handle the physics, and let learning handle the strategy.
